item.title: There is No Point in Compilers, OS or Static Code Anymore.
item.description:
Prefer listening? This article is also available as an audio version on YouTube.

The Future is Now

A bit more than a year ago, I wrote an essay with my thoughts on the agentic coding wave that was only starting to gain traction back then. My main conclusion was that at some point in the future, we would have to pass our own nurturing love for programming to the AI completely. And when that happens, there will be no way back, because the machine will eventually do things that people cannot truly understand in their full capacity, as the sheer amount and complexity of code produced will simply be impractical for a human brain to comprehend.

For better or worse this day has come.

The best coding models assisted with the best harnesses are already better at writing clean code, debugging, researching, and keeping tons of boring routine stuff in place than most human programmers. Furthermore, they never get tired, bored, or lack pedanticity. It is not necessary to list here all the impressive things AI has achieved in recent months, as I am pretty sure anybody reading this is already well aware of it. People can simply no longer track this entire code production factory completely, and we just hope that the agent did its best most of the time.

Now, this shift is starting to break all the assumptions that were put into software development over the decades. It started with the so-called SaaS-pocalypse, where almost anyone can vibe-code any service they need in an afternoon, and it leads straight to a much more fundamental question: why do models still have to output human-readable code if no human is ever going to read it anyway?

The Post-Compiler Era

Ever since the stored-program computer was described in 1945, the code executed on the processing unit has been a mostly static, pre-built binary stored in memory. It had to contain a massive amount of fallback cases for different types of hardware and architectures to be supported. For more than eighty years, this assumption held, largely because it was the only way to keep the ever-growing complexity of computing systems manageable by a limited human brain. We built compilers, runtime environments, and operating systems because humans could never hope to write raw, optimal machine code on the fly.

I would like to argue that the code of tomorrow is never stored in memory. Some pieces of it, templates and reusable structural elements, will endure, but not all of it.

Code, if you can even call it that anymore, is going to be written and executed on the fly by an AI system that exists on a dedicated neural processing unit, using the CPU and GPU as a pure processing power warehouse to calculate what is needed and produce an output for the end user. It will generate pure instructions in the native binary format, sent to the hardware in just enough quantity to make it busy enough to think about the current task and prepare the next batch of instructions, exactly in a form the processing units expect them.

Not in the Cloud

When we imagine this kind of future, the immediate temptation is to picture today’s massive frontier models sitting in the cloud, writing scripts and managing our devices. But a static, cloud-tethered model is fundamentally incapable of acting as the substrate for personal computing.

Every standard large language model we have today is a frozen snapshot. It was trained once at astronomical cost, cast in digital stone, and shipped with a hard cutoff date. It knows nothing about the specific machine in front of you, the timing of your memory bus, or the rhythm of what you are doing right now. Even with the local model and a powerful harness like Hermes that already went quite close to the adaptable personal agent, at the moment you try to fine-tune its brain - typical static LLM on your daily tasks, it forgets what it knew before. A frozen model living in a remote data center is even worse at organically adapt to your hardware or your life.

This flow of reasoning was a large part of why I started experimenting with mini-AGI. I wanted to see if it was possible to build a model that doesn’t rely on tokenizers, lives on modest consumer hardware, and learns continually from a single stream of raw bytes. A model like that is not meant to be just another chatbot, but an early proof of concept for the kind of adaptable, living neural core that could actually sit on local silicon and mediate between human intent and raw hardware. It was an enormous surprise to see it actually working the first time I stated training the model in the “impossible” (as I believed it) streaming regime and seeing that it still learns without much signs of “catastrophic forgetting” visible.

Ephemeral Instructions

In this new wave of computing, you simply do not need an operating system, a BIOS, static device drivers, or millions of lines of defensive code where ninety-nine percent of it sits completely dormant on disk.

The model does not need a human engineer to write an abstract driver layer to communicate with a graphics chip or a sensor. Because it operates at the raw byte level and learns continually, it can interact with the hardware directly, learn the timing and responses of the silicon through execution feedback, and discover the most efficient instruction paths on its own.

When you want to accomplish something, the system does not load an application binary from a drive. It understands your intent, synthesizes the exact machine instructions required for that specific microsecond, sends them to the execution warehouse, and the code immediately evaporates the moment the result is computed. It existed only for the brief moment it was needed, tailored perfectly to the state of the machine at that exact point in time. It is extremely efficient, and completely alien to how we have thought about software for the last eighty years.

New Species

For generations, we have treated personal computers as rigid, predictable, somewhat boring appliances. You buy a box with frozen specifications, install an operating system stamped out in a corporate factory, run static programs written by strangers until you eventually replace it with better cold box, keeping only the data it had, but never the experiences it lived through.

As we move toward continual, hardware-native intelligence, personal computers stop looking like boring machines and start looking much more like living, adaptable organisms that live alongside us.

Instead of setting up software, you will essentially be adopting an unformed digital nervous system that maps its own hardware and begins adapting to your life. It will evolve its own internal pathways, synthesize the tools you need out of thin air, and quietly discard what it no longer uses. It will carry no corporate agenda and no frozen legacy assumptions, because its entire existence is shaped by your data and your machine. It marks the moment computing stops being a cold, static tool we operate, and becomes a genuine, living extension of our own minds.

And you know what the craziest thing about all of this is?

It is going to happen much sooner than we all expect. For my personal estimate, I give it just two more years until something like this actually starts appearing on the mass market.

item.title: The Sunset of Human-Readable Code.
item.description:
Introduction

There’s a shift happening in the world of programming right now, at this very moment. It feels deeper and more fundamental than anything that happened before. It’s a change in the very nature of how we create software, driven by the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) in code generation. And as someone who has loved the craft of programming — the intricate logic, the elegant structures, the deep understanding required — I feel we’re standing nearby a dramatic transition, looking out at a future both majestic and horrifying.

The programming I knew, the kind that demanded you hold complex systems within your mind, is changing. Tools like Copilot and its increasingly sophisticated successors are becoming ubiquitous. More and more, our role is shifting. We are less the meticulous architects drawing every line, and more like pilots or shepherds, guiding powerful LLM agents, trying to keep them on track, nudging them away from breaking things too severely.

From Architect to AI Whisperer

Think about the traditional process: absorbing requirements, designing data structures and algorithms, carefully crafting functions and classes, debugging subtle interactions and trying to find the time for so bloody needed refactoring. There was an inherent incentive, almost a necessity, to maintain a holistic understanding of the project’s structure. Your mind was the primary repository for all of that.

Now, that incentive is fading. Why spend hours meticulously mapping out a complex module when an LLM can generate a plausible version in seconds? The focus shifts from deep construction to high-level direction and validation. We feed the AI prompts, review the output, iterate, and integrate. It’s undeniably faster for many tasks, capable of producing boilerplate or even complex algorithms we might have struggled with. But with this speed comes a subtle erosion of that deep, internalised understanding. We are becoming experts at driving the AI, but perhaps less expert in the underlying terrain it traverses.

The Seductive Path of Trust and Obscurity

Today, LLM-generated code often requires careful scrutiny. It fails in subtle ways, introduces security flaws, or misunderstands complex requirements. We are still the necessary gatekeepers, the human-in-the-loop ensuring quality.

But the trajectory is clear. LLMs are improving at an astonishing rate. With each iteration, they become more capable, their failures less frequent, their outputs more robust. As this happens, our trust inevitably grows. We’ll spend less time reviewing, more time accepting the generated code. The “good enough” becomes “surprisingly good,” and eventually, perhaps, “consistently better than I could do alone in the same timeframe”.

This increasing reliance is a one-way street. The more we trust the AI, the less comprehensively we understand the systems being built. Project complexity can balloon, supported by AI-generated scaffolding that no single human fully grasps. It will simply work, most of the time.

The Linguistic Singularity

This leads to the most radical and unsettling part of this transformation. Once AI can generate robust, well-behaved code almost perfectly, the constraints of human-readable programming languages becomes a liability.

Why force an AI, capable of processing information in ways we can barely imagine, to express its logic in syntaxes designed for human cognition (like Python, Java, or Rust)? The next logical step is for programming languages — or whatever replaces them — to adapt towards the AI.

Imagine languages optimised not for human eyes, but for maximum efficiency in AI generation, verification, and execution. They might look like incomprehensible “gibberish” to us — dense, symbolic, perhaps multi-dimensional data structures rather than linear text. These new forms of “code” would be incredibly efficient, highly optimised, inherently less prone to certain types of errors, and performant beyond our current benchmarks.

But they would be utterly alien. We would quickly find ourselves in a situation where comprehending the generated code, even if we desperately wanted to, becomes impractical, then difficult, and finally, fundamentally impossible. The very concept of “reading the source” could become meaningless.

Beyond Code Itself: The AI Mind Simulation

Taking this speculation a step further, perhaps the notion of a distinct “programming language” itself dissolves. Future AI systems might not need to explicitly generate code in any intermediate format. They could potentially simulate the desired system directly within their own complex internal states, manifesting the results directly as functional behaviour or user interfaces — the “pretty graphics” we interact with.

There would be no source code to inspect, no language to learn. Just an input (our request) and an output (the working software or system), with an impenetrable, hyper-complex process happening within the AI’s “mind.” We would interact with technology whose inner workings are not just unknown, but potentially unknowable by the human intellect.

Not Our Future

There’s a terrifying grandeur to this potential future. Imagine complex global systems — logistics, scientific research, resource management — running with near-perfect efficiency, orchestrated by AI far exceeding human capabilities. Problems currently intractable could be solved. This is the majestic part.

The horror lies in the loss of understanding, control, and agency. We become entirely dependent on systems we cannot interrogate, debug, or truly direct. What happens when these perfectly optimised, incomprehensible systems exhibit emergent behaviour we didn’t anticipate? Who fixes the unreadable “gibberish” when the AI fails in a novel way? Does the craft of programming, as a human endeavour of creation and understanding, simply cease to exist?

I don’t have the answers. But I feel this transition viscerally, right now. The way I write code, think about systems, and even identify as a programmer is evolving under the immense gravity of AI. It’s exciting, promising, and deeply unsettling all at once. The programming I knew and loved is changing, fundamentally and irrevocably. There’s likely no going back.

It seems, we are the last generation that have seen a miracle of human-readable code.
